entry.title: Prompt Acceptance Criteria: the fastest way to get reliable AI outputs
entry.summary: If you’ve ever thought “the model ignored what I said”, there’s a good chance you didn’t actually say it in a way that can be checked. Most prompts describe intent (what you want) but skip acceptance criteria (how to tell it’s done). In software, we don’t ship “make it nicer” — we ship “passes these tests”. Prompting works the same way. This post is a practical pattern I use constantly: Write the acceptance criteria first. Then write the prompt. It sounds boring. It’s also the fastest way to turn flaky outputs into repeatable results. Acceptance criteria are verifiable requirements for the output. They answer: What must be included? What must be excluded? What format should the answer have? What quality bar should it meet? How will I quickly review it? When you include these, you’re not “o…

Recently I needed to process incoming emails automatically. The idea sounded simple: Email arrives → extract some fields → trigger a webhook Things like: order confirmations

entry.title: 🛠️ I Built a One-Click ComfyUI Setup for RTX 5090 on Windows — No WSL2, No Docker
entry.summary:
I bought an RTX 5090. 32GB VRAM. The most powerful consumer GPU on the planet. Then I tried to run ComfyUI on Windows. It broke immediately. RuntimeError: sm_120 is not compatible
Three days later, I had a fully working solution. I packaged it and open-sourced it: ComfyUI-Win-Blackwell Here's the whole story. NVIDIA's Blackwell architecture (RTX 5090/5080/5070) uses a new compute capability code called sm_120. The problem? PyTorch's stable release doesn't include kernels for it. This means: pip install torch → doesn't work on Blackwell
